chapter: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
title: Regret at no formal teacher; Billy Aradonna
summary: Smith thinks a teacher might have helped his tone but he would still have come home, as trumpeter Billy Aradonna did.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you think that if you had studied saxophone with sort of a professional teacher, you might have been a better player?
For instance, it's sometimes said of you that your tone could have been stronger.
Do you regret not having done that?

Well, in a way, I have. And in a way, again, I think it wouldn't have been no use, that I would probably have ended up the same. I would have got tired of it and come on back home, like some of the rest of the boys. Like Billy Aradonna(?) has done...
Billy Aradonna(?). He's a great trumpet player. He plays that old-timey (?) and he loved Louis Armstrong's style. He's back here, and he's still... He's around the corner. But he
don't go nowhere to stay. He's still.
I don't know this man's name. Can you say it again?

Billy Aradonna(?). He played with Benny Carter a while. He came back here and started working in the Post Office. He's retired now. I think he retired last year. He worked there about 15 or 20 years. But it was mostly ...(? )...(? )... to see what could be done with enough music.
But it's interesting that you would get a piano, and you literally found the notes to the chords just by ear -- just by hearing the sound.

Yes, just by hearing the sound. Yes, just by hearing the sound. And then, of course, the way you voice your chords, voice the notes, make them sound different, and give the big sound and the little sound, or whatever... You can do that on a piano, but you can't do it on no horn, because you're only playing one note at a time.
